name: component-configurator
intent: Link and unlink component implementations in a running application from an external configuration script, so the set of services and their implementations can be composed, replaced or removed at run time without modifying, recompiling, relinking or restarting the executable.
problem: The component set a process should run is deployment-specific or changes while it runs - a new protocol handler, a different storage backend, an upgraded service, a per-customer feature - yet implementations are compiled into the executable and wired at link time, so every change means rebuild, relink and restart. For a high-availability server a restart is downtime, and for a product line it multiplies builds.
context: Long-running, availability-critical applications (servers, middleware, daemons, telecom and industrial systems) that must be composed - and recomposed - while they run, on platforms that expose a dynamic linking facility: shared libraries and dlopen-style APIs, JVM class loaders and module layers, .NET load contexts, Apple bundles, or a language's own module/require mechanism. The pattern assumes a stable component contract, components packaged as separately deployable units, and a trusted configuration source.
benefits: Runtime composition: components are linked, initialised, suspended and unlinked while the process keeps serving, so installing or replacing a service no longer needs a restart window.

One generic executable per product family: the deployment-specific composition lives in a configuration script, not in a build variant, so packaging and qualification shrink to one binary plus a per-deployment script.
The core stays closed for modification: a new component is a new loadable unit and a script entry, with no edit to the core and no relink.

Centralised identity and lifecycle: one repository knows every configured component, its instance and its state, so lookup, iteration, suspend/resume and dependency-ordered teardown happen in a single place.
A uniform component contract (interface plus lifecycle hooks) keeps implementations interchangeable and keeps the configurator independent of what it loads.
Operational control: composition becomes data that operators can review, version, stage and roll back independently of a code release.
tradeoffs: ABI and toolchain coupling: because the binding happens at run time, host and component must agree on symbol names, type layout, runtime and compiler versions, and mismatches surface at load time in production rather than at compile time (Go demands an identical toolchain, C++ mangling must be bridged, Swift protocol/ABI versions must match, .NET can silently load a duplicate contract assembly).

Unlink is the hard half: unloading is only safe after every reference is gone (dlclose reference counts and RTLD_GLOBAL symbol retention, JVM class loaders that must become unreachable, .NET collectible contexts pinned by lingering references), and several runtimes cannot unload at all - so 'reconfiguration' quietly degrades into restart-based deployment.

The configuration script becomes a critical, unvalidated artifact: it decides which code runs in the process, so a typo, a stale path or a writable configuration directory turns into an outage or a code-execution vector, and it needs the review, versioning and tests normally reserved for code.

More moving parts and one more indirection than a composition root: configuration parser, repository, lifecycle state machine and symbol/handle lookup all have to be designed and operated, and a fault can originate in the script, the loader, the contract version or the component itself.

Failures migrate to load time and are harder to diagnose: missing symbols, version skew, duplicate contracts and symbol shadowing between components appear as load-time errors or crashes whose stack trace starts in code that was not compiled with the host.

Portability of the infrastructure itself: the linking facility is platform-specific, so the configurator needs a wrapper facade per platform, and runtimes without a stable ABI force an out-of-process or C-ABI boundary that changes the performance and failure profile.

participants.responsibility: Defines the uniform interface every component implementation provides - usually an abstract class or function table carrying lifecycle hooks (init, fini, optionally suspend/resume) plus the service operations - so the configurator and the rest of the system can treat all components polymorphically.

Implements the Component interface, is packaged as a separately loadable unit (shared library, bundle, assembly, module, jar) and may offer additional interfaces; it never learns how it was linked into the process.

Manages the components currently configured into the process: keeps the name-to-component map, tracks whether each entry is initialised, suspended or unlinked, and provides lookup, iteration and state queries for the configurator and the application.

Interprets the configuration script or file and drives the component life cycle - linking implementations through the platform's dynamic linking facility, inserting them into the repository, initialising, suspending, resuming and unlinking them - hiding the linker behind a uniform interface.

use_cases: High-availability servers that must upgrade, replace or reconfigure services without dropping in-flight requests (transaction processing, telecom switching, industrial process control).
Middleware and daemons that compose their service set at start-up from a configuration file: protocol stacks, logging handlers, security services, storage backends, device drivers.
Product lines and embedded devices where one generic binary is configured per product or licence by a per-product script instead of one build per composition.

Plugin hosts that must also remove a component at run time: suspending a misbehaving implementation, loading a corrected version and resuming, or releasing a component's memory when it is no longer licensed.

Systems that must move a component instance between processes or threads - or replicate it into several processes - without shutting the running processes down, which is the reconfiguration goal POSA2 states for the pattern.
Test and developer environments where the same executable runs different component sets per configuration, shortening the loop between changing a component and seeing it run.

Eclipse IDE and other Rich Client Platforms built on OSGi/Equinox, where the entire application is a dynamically configured bundle composition started from a configuration file (plugin.xml, MANIFEST.MF), enabling installation of new features without restarting the workbench.

Redis database modules (Redis Stack, RedisGears) that register command handlers, data types, and filters at runtime through a module API discovered and loaded via configuration rather than compiled into the server binary.

Enterprise integration frameworks (Apache Camel, CXF) that compose routes, endpoints, and data format handlers from a DSL or XML configuration at startup, enabling a single JVM to host different integration flows per deployment.

Kubernetes operator frameworks (Operator SDK, Kubebuilder) where custom controller logic is loaded as an out-of-process sidecar or in-process plugin to extend the control plane without modifying the core Kubernetes binary.

telecom prepaid billing platforms and SS7 SIGTRAN nodes where protocol handlers (MAP, CAP, INAP) are loaded from configuration at process start, enabling a single binary to serve different network operators with different protocol stacks.

NGINX, which since 1.9.11 loads dynamic modules as shared objects named by load_module directives in the main context of nginx.conf, resolving them with dlopen at startup and configuration reload and keeping a module that appears in both the old and new configuration mapped across the reload - composition of the request-processing pipeline driven entirely by the configuration file.

Apache HTTP Server, where the statically-linked mod_so reads LoadModule directives from httpd.conf and links each module - including the MPM itself (mpm_event_module, mpm_worker_module, mpm_prefork_module) - as a Dynamic Shared Object, so one httpd binary runs a different component set per deployment, selected by configuration rather than by build variant.

Envoy proxy dynamic modules, which load shared objects at runtime from bootstrap or xDS configuration behind a hash-verified C ABI, resolved via ENVOY_DYNAMIC_MODULES_SEARCH_PATH and dlopened RTLD_LOCAL by default, extending HTTP filters, network filters, tracers and load balancers without recompiling the proxy.
avoid_when: The composition is fixed and known at build time: a composition root (explicit wiring, constructor injection, a factory) is simpler, compile-checked and carries no ABI surface.
The process is short-lived or restarts are cheap: the linker, repository and script machinery buys nothing over simply starting the new binary.

The runtime cannot unload code and hot replacement is the goal (Go plugins, JavaScript/Python/Ruby module caches, non-collectible .NET contexts): deployment by restart, or components out of process, is the honest answer.
Isolation rather than configurability is the requirement: put the component behind a process or network boundary (service, sidecar, XPC) so a faulty component cannot take the host down with it.
The variation is per request rather than per deployment: selecting behaviour from configuration with a strategy or a feature toggle is the right scope - linking code is the wrong tool.

The platform forbids or audits runtime code loading (signed or notarised application bundles, managed runtimes with locked loaders, read-only container images): the operational and security cost of an exception usually exceeds the flexibility it buys.
anti_patterns: "Configuration" that is still compiled in: #ifdefs, a switch over built-in implementations or a build-time property - the application is reconfigured by rebuilding, which is exactly what the pattern exists to remove.

Unlink without draining: releasing a component while callbacks, threads, event subscriptions or cached function pointers into it are still live, so the process crashes later in code that no longer exists.

No dependency order and no rollback: components linked and initialised in file order, so a failure half-way through leaves the repository holding handles to components that were never initialised and leaks the rest.

Treating the configuration script as an afterthought: unversioned, unvalidated, edited in place on a live system and loaded from a writable directory, so a typo becomes an outage and the script becomes a code-injection vector.
Using the repository as a global service locator, so components fetch each other at call time and every dependency is discoverable only by watching production.
Rebuilding the pattern on a runtime that deliberately forbids run-time linking (Go's plugin package, Rust dylibs) instead of moving the component out of process where it can be replaced by restart.

DLL search order hijacking: loading components via relative paths or system-search-path DLLs lets an attacker place a malicious library earlier in the search order, executing arbitrary code inside the host process with the host's privileges.

ClassCastException across classloader boundaries in JVM: when two components share a class name (e.g. com.example.Model) loaded by different classloaders, an instance from one classloader cannot be cast to the type from another, even if the bytecode is identical - this surfaces as a runtime crash rather than a compile-time error.

Silent duplicate contract assembly in .NET: if a component bundles its own copy of the contract assembly, the host may load the component's copy instead of its own, causing type mismatches at cast or method-call time that are extremely difficult to diagnose.
design_principles: Dependency inversion: the configurator and the repository depend on the Component abstraction and on a uniform loading interface; components depend only on the published contract.
Open/closed principle: new components arrive as new loadable units declared in the configuration, while the executable stays closed for modification and needs no relink.

Separation of concerns: configuration policy (the script), the linking mechanism (a wrapper facade over the platform's linker) and component behaviour are three separate concerns with three separate owners.
Information hiding: a component never knows how it was linked, and the rest of the system never knows which loader or namespace performed the linking.
Single responsibility with an explicit life cycle: the repository owns identity and state, the configurator owns the script and the link/unlink sequence, and each component owns its own resources.
Fail fast at the boundary: validate the configuration and the component's contract before mutating the running composition, not after the first request reaches the new component.

Principle of least privilege for the configuration source: the directory containing component implementations and the configuration script should be non-writable by the process at runtime, preventing an attacker who compromises the process from injecting new code or altering the composition.
best_practices: Publish a narrow, versioned component contract - lifecycle hooks plus the service interface - in an artifact shared by host and component, and verify the version when linking.
Parse and validate the whole configuration before executing it, and make reconfiguration atomic: build the new composition, then swap it in, or roll back to the previous one.

Keep one repository as the single source of truth (name to implementation, handle and state) and route every link, initialise, suspend, resume and unlink through it so no caller can bypass the life cycle.
Drain before unlink: remove registrations, stop threads, wait for in-flight calls and then release the implementation in reverse dependency order, with a finalize hook in the component contract.

Bind strictly and isolate: resolve symbols when loading (RTLD_NOW-style), keep component namespaces local (RTLD_LOCAL, separate class loaders or load contexts), and load only from trusted, non-writable locations with a validated list.

Treat the configuration as code: version it, smoke-test every supported composition in CI, and log life-cycle events (linked, initialised, suspended, unlinked, failed) with the component name and version.
Prefer an out-of-process boundary for components you do not fully trust or that cannot be unloaded: replacing a process is a solved problem, replacing loaded code is not.

Harden the DLL search order: use absolute paths to component implementations, remove the current working directory from the search path, and on Windows call SetDllDirectory (or the equivalent) to eliminate search order hijacking vectors.

Prevent classloader leaks on the JVM: ensure no static references to component classes, clear ThreadLocal values in the component's fini() hook, remove all thread stacks from any component-managed ExecutorService, and break any WeakHashMap reference chains that reach the component's classloader before declaring it unreachable.

Verify contract compatibility before linking: on .NET, use AssemblyLoadContext to isolate components and prevent the host from accidentally resolving to a component-bundled copy of the contract assembly; on Java, use a dedicated classloader per component with a shared interface-classloader for the contract.

Log load-time failures with full context: the component path, the resolved symbol name, the ABI versions of both host and component, and the full exception chain - because these failures are notoriously difficult to reproduce in a development environment.

Instrument the lifecycle state machine with a state-of-truth log (linked, init_failed, active, suspended, draining, unlinking, unloaded) so operational staff and automated monitors can observe the composition state without introspecting the repository directly.
sources: Schmidt, Stal, Rohnert & Buschmann, Pattern-Oriented Software Architecture Vol. 2: Patterns for Concurrent and Networked Objects (Wiley, 2000) - Component Configurator, in chapter 2, Service Access and Configuration Patterns.

Schmidt, D.C., 'The Service Configurator Framework: An Extensible Framework for Dynamic Configuration of Concurrent Distributed Services' (Department of Computer Science, College of William & Mary), https://www.cs.wm.edu/~schmidt/PDF/service-configurator.pdf - the original ACE Service Configurator paper that is the C++ reference implementation of the POSA2 pattern.
POSA2 Pattern Abstracts, Vanderbilt University, https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/POSA/POSA2/pattern-abstracts.html
POSA2 Service Access and Configuration Patterns, Vanderbilt University, https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/POSA/POSA2/access-patterns.html
POSA2 Home Page, Vanderbilt University, https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/~schmidt/POSA/POSA2/

ACE+TAO Overview, Vanderbilt University, https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu - documents the ACE framework that implements the Component Configurator pattern as the ACE_Service_Config class, used in The ACE ORB (TAO) for telecom and aerospace middleware.

OSGi Alliance, OSGi Core Release 7 Specification, https://www.osgi.org - the authoritative specification for the OSGi component model, a widely deployed Java implementation of the Component Configurator pattern with dynamic bundle lifecycle management.

Eclipse Equinox, The Eclipse Foundation, https://wiki.eclipse.org/Equinox - Eclipse's OSGi implementation that demonstrates the pattern in a production IDE and RCP application context, with support for dynamic bundle installation and startup without restart.

Java Service Loader SPI Documentation, Oracle/OpenJDK, https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ext/basics/spi.html - a simpler, less lifecycle-rich sibling of Component Configurator that discovers implementations at load time but does not support unloading; useful for SPI discovery but insufficient for true dynamic reconfiguration.

Managed Extensibility Framework (MEF), Microsoft Learn, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/framework/extensibility/ - .NET's built-in implementation of a component discovery and composition model that approximates the Component Configurator pattern using AssemblyLoadContext for isolation and catalog-based component registration.

Linux man7.org, dlopen(3) manual page, https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/dlopen.3.html - documents the POSIX dynamic linking API (dlopen, dlsym, dlclose, dlerror) that underpins Component Configurator implementations on Linux, including the RTLD_NOW, RTLD_LOCAL, and RTLD_GLOBAL flags critical for safe component isolation.

Microsoft Security Response Center, 'Secure loading of libraries to prevent DLL preloading attacks', https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/dlls/secure-loading-of-libraries - documents the DLL search order hijacking attack surface that Component Configurator implementations on Windows must guard against, and the SetDllDirectory API as a mitigation.
Baeldung, 'Java Service Provider Interface (SPI)', https://www.baeldung.com/java-spi - practical guide to Java's ServiceLoader mechanism and its relationship to the Component Configurator pattern.

Apache Camel Documentation, Component Configuration, https://camel.apache.org - an enterprise integration framework that exemplifies the pattern: a single JVM hosts different sets of routes, components, and data formats composed entirely from configuration files.

Schmidt & Hust, C++ Network Programming, Volume 2: Systematic Reuse with ACE and Frameworks (Wiley, 2003), Chapter 5 'The ACE Service Configurator Framework', https://www.cs.wm.edu/%7Edcschmidt/ACE/book2/c5.html - the framework-level treatment of the pattern: decoupling service behaviour from the timing of its configuration, developed around a networked logging server.

ACE+TAO Doxygen, 'Service_Config.h File Reference' (ACE 8.0.2), https://www.dre.vanderbilt.edu/Doxygen/8.0.2/html/libace-doc/a00974.html - current reference documentation for ACE_Service_Config (aliased ACE_Component_Config) and the ACE_STATIC/DYNAMIC/VERSIONED/REMOVE_SERVICE_DIRECTIVE macros that express svc.conf link, suspend and unlink directives, confirming the pattern's canonical C++ implementation remains maintained.

NGINX Documentation, 'Dynamic Modules', https://docs.nginx.com/nginx/admin-guide/dynamic-modules/dynamic-modules/ - official documentation of the load_module directive that loads .so modules into nginx from nginx.conf at startup and configuration reload, a production example of configuration-script-driven component composition in a web server.

Apache HTTP Server Documentation, 'Dynamic Shared Object (DSO) Support', https://httpd.apache.org/docs/current/dso.html - official docs for mod_so and LoadModule-driven module linking, including MPMs selected as DSOs by configuration rather than by build - the web server's long-standing production use of the pattern.

Envoy Documentation, 'Dynamic modules', https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/advanced/dynamic_modules - official documentation of runtime-loaded shared-object extensions behind a hash-verified C ABI with RTLD_LOCAL default loading, search-path resolution and explicit load-failure handling.

PostgreSQL Documentation, 'Runtime Configuration - Client Connection Defaults', https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html - shared_preload_libraries, session_preload_libraries and local_preload_libraries load C extension libraries named in configuration at server or session start, and the server refuses to start when a listed library cannot be found: fail-fast composition taken from a production database server.

Kishore Ganesh, 'Why did dlclose not unload the library?', https://kishoreganesh.com/post/why-dl-close-did-not-work/ - practical analysis of why dlclose frequently does not unmap code (RTLD_GLOBAL symbol retention, the NODELETE flag, pending thread-local storage destructors), documenting the main criticism that unlink - the pattern's promise of removal - is the unreliable half on real platforms.

related_patterns_notes.wrapper-facade: Provides the low-level API abstraction (dlopen/dlsym, LoadLibrary, classloaders) that the Component Configurator wraps behind its platform-independent facade, hiding the raw linking mechanism from the rest of the system.
related_patterns_notes.registry: The Component Repository is a specific instance of Registry that tracks live component instances by name and state, but adds lifecycle semantics (initialised, suspended, unlinked) that a generic key-value registry lacks.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: Component Configurator is the architecture that enables a Plugin system; the plugin pattern defines the contract for discoverable, loadable extensions while the configurator provides the runtime wiring and lifecycle management infrastructure.
related_patterns_notes.acceptor-connector: Acceptor-Connector decouples connection establishment from service handling in networked applications; when a service handler itself is a dynamically loaded component, the Connector can request the Component Configurator to link in the appropriate handler implementation before passing the connection.
related_patterns_notes.extension-interface: Both patterns from POSA2 address extensibility without recompilation; Extension Interface allows a component to expose multiple versioned interfaces to prevent interface bloat, while Component Configurator manages the runtime loading/unloading that makes those interfaces available at all - they are often used together in the same system.
related_patterns_notes.interceptor: Interceptors observe or modify invocations at runtime; when components are dynamically loaded via Component Configurator, the interceptor registration (on init) and deregistration (on fini) become part of the component's lifecycle hooks, so the two patterns interoperate at the lifecycle boundary.
related_patterns_notes.service-locator: Both maintain a registry of available services, but Service Locator is a run-time query pattern (components call in to find collaborators) while Component Configurator is a run-time wiring pattern (the host assembles components from outside); using the repository as a service locator is an anti-pattern that creates hidden coupling and blocks safe unlink.
related_patterns_notes.dependency-injection: Dependency Injection composes an application's graph at construction time, often via a container; Component Configurator composes the same graph at runtime via external configuration - the patterns address the same problem at different timescales, and hybrid approaches use DI containers to wire individual dynamically-loaded components internally while the configurator manages which components are loaded.
